incidente.resumo: After the passwords for the vSphere account were rotated, the vsphere-janitor service's configuration was not updated, so it could not authenticate or clean up build VMs, and VMs leaked until new build VMs could not power on, causing instability and outage of Travis CI's OS X build environment. Service was restored by fixing the configuration, restarting the service, aggressively cleaning up leaked VMs, running at reduced capacity, and later changing the CPU reservation configuration.
servicos_afetados: OS X build environment for open source and private repositories

descricao.texto: The team became aware of higher than normal re-queue rates for builds on the OS X platform, leading to a large backlog; the text does not say how this was noticed. Existing VM-count alerting did not trigger.
trechos: We became aware of higher than normal re-queue rates for builds on our OS X platform, which were leading to a large backlog of OS X builds.
But due to this defect in the software, the alerts did not trigger because the metric kept being reporting at a number which was within our *good* range.

gatilho.texto: On Friday, July 31st, the passwords for the vSphere account that the services use to authenticate with the vSphere API were rotated in response to vSphere's default 90 day password expiration policy.
trechos: A this point we recalled we had rotated the passwords for the vSphere account that our services use to authentication with the vSphere API, on the previous Friday, July 31st, in response to vSphere's default 90 day password expiration policy.

descricao.texto: When the rotation happened, the configuration for the vsphere-janitor service, which is responsible for the final cleanup phase of build VMs, did not get updated; the service was unable to authenticate and so could not clean up any build VMs, and VMs leaked from 2015-07-31 to 2015-08-04.
trechos: When the rotation happened,  the configuration for the *vsphere-janitor* service did not get updated.
This resulted in the service being unable to authenticate and so it was unable to cleanup any build VMs.
We then began *leaking* VMs, from 2015-07-31 to 2015-08-04 when we discovered the configuration issue.

Due to the nature of what information we can get from the vSphere APIs and the long build timeouts we provide for travis-ci.com private repositories, we have a specialized service (*vsphere-janitor*) which is responsible for the final cleanup phase of build VMs.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: A defect in vsphere-janitor made it keep reporting the last detected number of total VMs to metrics storage when unable to authenticate, instead of reporting 0, so existing alerting on VM counts did not trigger because the metric stayed within the good range.
trechos: Which was that it will continue to report the last detected number of total VMs to our metrics storage, when it is unable authenticate, instead of reporting 0.
But due to this defect in the software, the alerts did not trigger because the metric kept being reporting at a number which was within our *good* range.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: Over 6000 virtual machines accumulated on the Xserve cluster versus no more than 200 at normal peak, and new VM power-on events failed because the vSphere cluster could not satisfy the resource reservations needed.
trechos: When we reviewed the resource utilization on our vSphere infrastructure, we discovered we had over **6000** virtual machines on the Xserve cluster.
During normal peak build times, this number shouldn't be more than **200**.
The power-on events were failing because the vSphere cluster was unable to satisfy the resource reservations needed to allow the VMs to power-on.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: A portion of the leaked VMs were in an unexpected state that caused the normal cleanup to skip them, because they had been leaked due to a failure to power-on rather than being ready for deletion in the normal lifecycle; the number of leaked VMs was too high for the cleanup process to handle with other builds running.
trechos: While monitoring the progress of the cleanup, we realized that the number of *leaked VMs* was simply too high for our cleanup process to handle with other builds running and that a portion of the very abnormally high number of *leaked VMs* were in an unexpected state.

They were in a state that caused our cleanup to skip them, because they had been *leaked* due to a failure to power-on and not because they were ready to be deleted as part of the normal build VM lifecycle.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: Power-on failures for new build VMs continued after all leaked VMs were deleted: the way CPU Reservations were configured meant the configured maximum number of builds could not actually be booted because there were not enough CPU cycles on the cluster. Normal peak loads had not reached this point; the large backlog from the incident hit the maximum for the first time.
trechos: At 22:56 UTC, when we began resuming builds we discovered, and very quickly started to see power-on failures for new build VMs, due to errors about a lack of the ability to satisfy the resource reservations of the new VMs.

What we were ultimately able to determine is that the way we had configured CPU Reservations for our build VMs resulted in a situation where when we tried to run the maximum number of builds we'd configured and assumed that we had capacity for, we were actually unable to actually boot that many VMs, because there were not enough CPU cycles available on the cluster.
It was only because of the large backlog that this incident had accrued, that we actually hit the maximum for the first time and uncovered this configuration limitation.

descricao.texto: Rotation of the passwords for the vSphere account used by the services to authenticate with the vSphere API, on July 31st, without updating the vsphere-janitor service configuration.
trechos: A this point we recalled we had rotated the passwords for the vSphere account that our services use to authentication with the vSphere API, on the previous Friday, July 31st, in response to vSphere's default 90 day password expiration policy.
When the rotation happened,  the configuration for the *vsphere-janitor* service did not get updated.

passos.texto: At 18:46 UTC all OS X builds were paused to stop all work on the infrastructure while investigating why vsphere-janitor was not deleting VMs.
trechos: At 18:46 UTC, we paused all OS X builds in order to stop all work on the infrastructure, we then dug into why *vsphere-janitor* was not properly deleting VMs.

passos.texto: The vsphere-janitor configuration issue was fixed and the service restarted, and it began cleaning up some of the backlog of build VMs; new builds stayed paused until 21:01 UTC, when builds for the .com queue were enabled while cleanup continued.
trechos: Once we realized the configuration issue, we fixed it, restarted the service, and it began cleaning up some of the backlog of build VMs.

We kept all new builds paused until 21:01 UTC to give the cleanup process some time to run, without competing for resources with new builds, and then enabled builds for the **.com** queue, will still running cleanup.

passos.texto: At 22:10 UTC all builds were paused again and a more aggressive cleanup mode that would also terminate new build VMs was run; it deleted all 6326 VMs.
trechos: In order to clean them up we needed to be able to run our cleanup in a mode that would also terminate new build VMs, so at 22:10 UTC we paused all builds again and initiated the more aggressive cleanup.
The cleanup proceeded successfully and quickly deleted all *6326* VMs.

passos.texto: When power-on failures reappeared, builds were paused again and at 23:28 UTC the infrastructure provider was contacted to help investigate the boot failures.
trechos: We once again paused all builds and at 23:28 UTC we reached out to our infrastructure provider to help investigate these boot failures.

passos.texto: After testing a reduced build throughput, both .com and .org builds were enabled at reduced capacity at 00:13 UTC, and the entire build backlog was processed at the reduced rate.
trechos: We determined we were able to operate at a reduced capacity and enabled both **.com** and **.org** builds, with the reduced capacity, at 00:13 UTC.
We operated at a reduced build rate and were able to successfully process the entire build backlog, with things remaining stable.

passos.texto: On Aug 06, 2015 at 03:43 UTC, builds were briefly paused and the recommended configuration changes to the CPU reservations were implemented: relying on virtual machine resource sizing instead of vSphere's resource reservation system. Builds were then resumed.
trechos: So on Aug 06, 2015 - 03:43 UTC, we briefly paused all OS X builds and implemented the recommended configuration changes to the CPU reservations.

MacStadium was able to help us understand that for our workload, we did not actually want to use the resource reservation system that vSphere implements but could just rely on the virtual machine resource sizing to sufficiently guarantee resources for each build VM.
We then resumed builds, caught up with the small backlog and began monitoring the infrastructure closely.

acoes.texto: Planned: more well defined load tests of the OS X infrastructure, including multiple build jobs representing common customer repository types and more detailed metrics gathered during the tests.
trechos: We are preparing plans for more well defined load tests of our OS X infrastructure.

This testing will include multiple build jobs that represent the common types of repositories we see customers building and we will have better and more detailed metrics that we'll gather during these load tests.

acoes.texto: Planned: improve the metrics collected when creating, running and deleting build VMs on the OS X infrastructure, and how these metrics are reported under failure conditions, to build better alerts.
trechos: We are going to make improvements to what metrics we collect when we create, run, and delete build VMs on the OS X infrastructure.
We will also improve how these metrics are reported under failure conditions.
These metrics improvements will help us build better alerts to help us avoid these kinds of issues in the future.

acoes.texto: Planned: improve how global stop/start of builds and re-queueing work so they have less impact on running builds, through improvements to the build agent software.
trechos: Some of the impact of this incident, in particular how we do a global stop/start of builds, and how they are re-queued, will be improved in ways that will result in less impact to running builds.
These will happen as we build and ship some fundamental improvements to our build agent software.

motivo_confianca_baixa: causa_raiz: the text describes two mechanisms (the un-updated vsphere-janitor credentials causing leaked VMs, and the CPU Reservations configuration causing boot failures that continued after the leaked VMs were deleted); the credential issue was chosen as root cause because it started the impact, and the CPU reservation issue went to fatores_contribuintes. deteccao: the text says the team 'became aware' of re-queue rates without saying how, so nao_informada was chosen over equipe_interna. duracao is null because the text gives no single start and end of the impact.
